title: Comparing in more than one direction
header: Comparing in more than one direction

text.text:
### Prerequisites

Before you continue, read **When size matters** (<htcite0>). There we learned to measure an object in one direction with a ruler, and we saw that two objects are fully equal only when they match in every characteristic we compare. This lesson continues that idea.

### Introduction

In the previous text we measured objects in one direction: we placed them on a ruler and read how long they are. But an object is not one-dimensional. It also has a width, a height, a color, a shape and a material, and each of these characteristics is another **direction** in which we can compare one object with another.

When we compare only the length, we learn only one part of the story. Two objects can have the same length and still be different in width, height or color.

Reflection 1: Should we measure in other directions?

We already know how to compare two objects in one direction by measuring their length. If the two objects have the same length, are they necessarily equal? Should we measure them in other directions, such as width, height and color, before deciding whether they are equal?

### Measuring in a New Direction

The good news is that we do not have to learn a new method. Measuring in another direction follows exactly the same steps we already used:

1. Choose the direction we want to compare — for example, the width.
2. Place both objects along the ruler so that one end of each object lines up with the mark of **0**.
3. Keep the objects straight in that direction and read the mark where each one stops.
4. Compare the two measures.

To compare the **width** of two objects, we measure them along the horizontal ruler. To compare their **height**, we measure them along the vertical ruler. To compare their **color**, we look at that characteristic and check whether both objects have the same color. In every case the method does not change: we choose a direction, measure both objects in that direction, and then compare the two measures.

When the two measures match, the objects are **equal in that direction**; when they differ, the objects are **different in that direction**. This is why two objects can be equal in one direction and different in another.

If we compare the objects in only one direction, we learn only part of the story. To say whether two objects are **fully equal**, we must repeat the same measurement in every direction that matters to us. The more directions we compare, the more complete our comparison becomes.

### Conclusion

In this lesson we learned that comparing does not stop at one direction. To compare two objects in a new direction, we repeat the same steps we already know: choose the direction, measure both objects in that direction, and compare the two measures. When the measures match, the objects are equal in that direction; when they differ, they are different in that direction.

We also saw that one direction is not enough. Two objects can have the same length and still differ in width, height or color. To decide whether two objects are **fully equal**, we must compare them in **every direction that matters to us**. The more directions we compare, the more complete — and the more trustworthy — our comparison becomes.
